title: Ethical principles for artificial intelligence in education
authors: Andy Nguyen, Ha Ngan Ngo, Yvonne Hong, Belle Dang, Bich‐Phuong Thi Nguyen
abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence in education (AIED) has the potential to transform the educational landscape and influence the role of all involved stakeholders. In recent years, the applications of AIED have been gradually adopted to progress our understanding of students' learning and enhance learning performance and experience. However, the adoption of AIED has led to increasing ethical risks and concerns regarding several aspects such as personal data and learner autonomy. Despite the recent announcement of guidelines for ethical and trustworthy AIED, the debate revolves around the key principles underpinning ethical AIED. This paper aims to explore whether there is a global consensus on ethical AIED by mapping and analyzing international organizations' current policies and guidelines. In this paper, we first introduce the opportunities offered by AI in education and potential ethical issues. Then, thematic analysis was conducted to conceptualize and establish a set of ethical principles by examining and synthesizing relevant ethical policies and guidelines for AIED. We discuss each principle and associated implications for relevant educational stakeholders, including students, teachers, technology developers, policymakers, and institutional decision-makers. The proposed set of ethical principles is expected to serve as a framework to inform and guide educational stakeholders in the development and deployment of ethical and trustworthy AIED as well as catalyze future development of related impact studies in the field.
explain_beginner: This paper looks at the rules different countries and organizations have made for using artificial intelligence in schools. The authors compared these policies and found that there is no single global agreement on what counts as ethical. Because of this, they combined the ideas into one shared set of ethical principles. This matters because AI is being used more and more in education, and it can affect students' private data and their freedom to learn in their own way. The authors hope their combined principles will help everyone involved build AI tools that are trustworthy.
explain_business: AI in education is spreading, and different regions follow different ethical rules, so there is no single global standard to rely on. This paper reviewed international policies and combined them into one set of ethical principles for AI in education. For executives, this means any AI learning product or institutional rollout should be checked against a shared ethical framework, not just local rules. The framework covers the interests of students, teachers, developers, policymakers, and institutional leaders. It informs decisions about which AI education tools to adopt, how to govern their use, and how to build trust with users and regulators.
explain_practitioner: The authors examined current policies and guidelines on ethical AI in education from international organizations to test whether a global consensus exists. They first reviewed the opportunities AIED offers and the ethical concerns it raises, such as issues around personal data and learner autonomy. They then applied thematic analysis to synthesize these policies into a conceptual set of ethical principles. The paper discusses each principle and its implications for students, teachers, developers, policymakers, and institutional decision makers. The resulting framework is intended to guide ethical and trustworthy development and deployment of AIED and to encourage future impact studies.
